source.title: Generalization Ability of Wide Neural Networks on ℝ
source.authors: Jian-Fa Lai; Manyun Xu; R. Chen; Qi-Rong Lin

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling affects the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own label-corruption experiments and argues that apparent benign overfitting depends on signal strength and the stopping rule, qualifying the generalization claim. The experiments do not directly test fitting completely random labels to zero training error.
record.gate_note: The paper’s theoretical and numerical results about one-dimensional regression, interpolation and label corruption bear on V4’s label-noise generalization claim. Figure 1’s randomly selected labels and Figure 2’s toy stopping-rule comparison are figure-only; they do not establish the complete-random-label fitting claim or its optimization-time version. No results test shuffled or Gaussian inputs, explicit regularization, or the real-label-first learning sequence.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 varies random label corruption and measures test performance during training, including stopping at near-zero training classification error. This bears on V4 over the tested corruption range. Its stopping-time comparisons do not themselves establish or contradict V4's degradation pattern.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' explanation, but should distinguish theorem from hypothesis. They prove optimal early-stopping rates and poor late-training generalization for specified wide two-layer networks on one-dimensional noisy regression data. They hypothesize, with illustrative synthetic and CIFAR-10 experiments, that signal strength determines whether near-perfect classification accuracy occurs near optimal stopping or near zero-loss stopping.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes wide two-layer ReLU networks in a lazy-training regime and reports separate synthetic and CIFAR-10 label-corruption experiments; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported gap between label-based and optimal stopping increases with label-corruption ratio; the authors hypothesize the relation depends on signal strength. Figure 3 reports squared-loss and cross-entropy experiments separately.

fits_no_version.finding: The gap between near-zero training classification error and optimal stopping increases with label corruption; the synthetic clean-label experiments show very small stopping-time and corresponding test-accuracy gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization of a classifier at near-perfect training accuracy depends on signal strength and its stopping time relative to optimal stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: For sufficiently wide two-layer ReLU networks in the specified one-dimensional noisy regression setting, late training approaches linear interpolation and has excess risk bounded away from zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation can be statistically inconsistent in low-dimensional noisy regression under lazy training.

record.peer_reviewed: Submitted to the Annals of Statistics; arXiv.org
record.problems: The label-corruption results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The synthetic experiment uses 100 training examples and 1000 test examples; the CIFAR-10 figure has no stated sample counts here. These experiments do not report training error at each corruption ratio.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 compares a four-point toy example under regression and classification and is described only as a stopping-rule illustration, not a label-corruption result; Figure 1 illustrates interpolation on equally spaced one-dimensional data with randomly selected labels, but does not test the claim’s random-label classification setting. Neither is included as a row.

untested.parts: Completely random classification labels, chance-level test error, and fitting with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters. Figure 1's random regression targets do not establish these conditions.
Time to fit completely random versus true labels, its constant-factor overhead, and convergence time versus corruption. A gap between two stopping rules is insufficient.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The full corruption range through p = 1 and the chance endpoint are untested. Separate measurements demonstrating capture of remaining signal while memorizing corrupted labels are not reported.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Separate learning trajectories for real patterns and noisy labels that establish which are learned first.

missing.what: Test accuracy at near-zero training classification error for each corruption level, separately for squared loss and cross-entropy, together with the achieved training error or stopping threshold. These are needed to assess V4; the extracted stopping-time gaps cannot substitute for them. The supplied text does not preserve readable plot values.

AlexNet training and test errors at label-based stopping for each corruption level, or readable generalization-gap values with their definition and training error. The supplied caption establishes only the stopping-time-gap trend.

record.verdict_notes: No V4 verdict is justified by the recorded stopping-time gaps alone. Poor generalization after fitting noise is compatible with V4, which already predicts worsening test performance. The supplied plain text omits the plotted values needed to assess its degradation pattern.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random training labels to zero or near-zero error with test error at chance, without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
The study does not compare training time to fit random labels with training time on true labels or report a small constant-factor cost.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

The paper varies label corruption and reports testing accuracy/loss or generalization-gap figures, but does not establish perfect training fit at each corruption level or show that networks capture remaining signal while memorizing noise.
No test of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
No measurement of whether real-data patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network (width m = 10000)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic data with label corruption using squared loss; compared stopping rules and reported test accuracy and loss.

conditions.value: Synthetic Data: 100 i.i.d. inputs from unif((0, 1)^3); 1000 testing data points

rows.measure: Testing accuracy and loss; relation between tlabel and topt
rows.value: Figure 3(a) only; text says the gap between tlabel and topt and between corresponding testing accuracies are extremely small when p = 0.
rows.note: The text describes the result but the figure supplies the values; the paper does not state a numerical accuracy or training error here.
rows.check: This is the clean-label control. A negligible difference between two stopping rules does not establish the effect of increasing corruption. Numerical training and test errors are not supplied.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic-data experiments at p = 0, 0.3 and 0.6, and AlexNet on CIFAR-10 at p = 0, 0.3 and 0.6
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the stopping-time gap grows with corruption and that near-zero label error can differ from near-zero loss; these results qualify a simple smooth-noise account, but do not establish perfect training fit or steadily rising test error (R1-R9).
